title: Professions and Institutional Change: Towards an Institutionalist Sociology of the Professions
author: Daniel Muzio · David M. Brock · Roy Suddaby

dom.t: Professional authority: AI enters an already contested field

st.t: Professional authority: AI enters an already contested field
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s authority-and-power framing by treating professions not merely as groups affected by change, but as institutional agents that create, maintain and disrupt governing arrangements within organisational contexts. This materially develops how professionals can shape legal-AI change, although the abstract alone provides a conceptual framework rather than AI-specific evidence or detailed empirical findings.

Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status

kp.k: Institutionalism offers a retheorization of contemporary professionalism
kp.d: Muzio, Brock and Suddaby propose an institutionalist perspective on professional work after critically reviewing functionalist and conflict-based approaches in the sociology of the professions. This is a theoretical contribution about professions generally, not a claim about AI or legal services specifically.
qs: we build on and further elaborate an > institutionalist perspective on professional work.
identifying a > functionalist and a conflict-based approach.

kp.k: Professions are institutions embedded in broader institutionalization
kp.d: The authors argue that professions should be studied as institutions and that professionalization should be connected to wider processes of institutionalization. Their framework places the development of professions within broader institutional change rather than treating professionalization as an isolated process.
qs: Such a perspective affirms the importance of > studying professions as institutions and connecting professionalization to broader patterns of > institutionalization;

kp.k: Professionals create, maintain and disrupt institutions
kp.d: The abstract treats professions and professionals as agents of institutional change, encompassing institutional maintenance as well as creation and disruption. The supplied gloss describes this agency using the vocabulary of institutional work and labels the special issue's consolidation of the professions–institutional theory merger as a reception note, rather than an abstract finding.
qs: it highlights the role of professions and professionals as agents in the > creation, maintenance, and disruption of institutions
in the vocabulary of institutional theory, carriers of institutional work

kp.k: Professionalization must account for organizational contexts
kp.d: The authors emphasize accommodating contemporary professionalization within organizational contexts. The accompanying reconstruction makes the stronger interpretation that organizations, rather than autonomous practitioners, are the setting for professional work and change; that formulation belongs to the supplied gloss, not the published abstract.
qs: recognizes the importance of > accommodating contemporary patterns of professionalization within the organizational context.
the organisation, not the autonomous practitioner, is where professional work and professional change now happen.

kp.k: Eight papers inform the special issue's theoretical synthesis
kp.d: The abstract states that eight special-issue papers advance empirical understanding of professional agency in contemporary change and contribute theoretically to reconceptualizing professionalism. The held document contains only the published abstract and a labeled reconstruction, so it supplies no individual study methods, samples or findings and does not substantiate specific effects of AI.
qs: We > also illustrate how, empirically, the eight papers in this issue advance our understanding of > professional agency in contemporary change

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Muzio, Brock and Suddaby offer an institutionalist account of professions and institutional change, not a claim about AI.
pts.d: In this cross-domain source, the authors connect professionalization to broader institutionalization, describe professionals as agents of institutional creation, maintenance and disruption, and emphasize the organizational context of professionalization. These are theoretical propositions rather than concrete predictions of technological or legal-market change. The supplied reconstruction's stronger assertion that organizations replace autonomous practitioners as the locus of professional change should not be treated as a verbatim claim from the abstract.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The stated basis is a theoretical review and a synthesis of eight special-issue papers; the held text supplies no specific empirical findings.
pts.d: The authors describe reviewing functionalist and conflict-based approaches, elaborating an institutionalist perspective, and drawing on eight papers for empirical and theoretical contributions. Only the abstract is held, so the studies' methods, cases and results cannot be extracted. No AI evidence is presented.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The argument concerns contemporary professionalism as discussed in the 2013 publication, without a forecast horizon.
pts.d: The organizational context is a stated consideration for understanding contemporary professionalization. The held text offers no dated prediction, adoption timetable or conditions under which AI would change professional services.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The account concerns professions and professionals broadly, situated within organizations and wider institutions.
pts.d: Professionals are presented as participants in institutional creation, maintenance and disruption, rather than merely recipients of change. The abstract does not distinguish legal-market segments, law-firm types, seniority levels, clients or the public, and it identifies no AI-related employment or service-delivery effects.
